# Making a wedged instance explain itself

Four admin diagnostics answer why an instance is stuck: which nodes are parked,
which frames are held, what the pending wakes are waiting for, and who holds the
claim. None of them requires opening the store.

## A deliberately wedged instance

A claim-holding node parks and does not come back, a second node co-holds its
claim, and a receiver declares a force-refreshed dependency on the parked node.

## Which nodes are parked

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/admin/diagnostics/parked-nodes"
rimsky parked list --endpoint "$BASE"
```

The roster names exactly the wedged node, identifies it as the claim holder, and
carries both when it parked and when it is due back — the reason and the
horizon, not just a name. The CLI verb returns the same row.

## Which frames are held

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/admin/diagnostics/held-frames"
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/instances/$IID/frames"
```

The roster reports one frame for the instance, names the parked node holding it,
reports its state as parked, and reports how long the frame has been held — the
signal that separates a wedge from ordinary in-flight work.

The same frame id appears on the instance's own frame listing, so the diagnostic
and the ordinary view agree.

## What the pending wakes are waiting for

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/admin/diagnostics/wait-sets?frame=$FRAME_ID"
```

The wait set carries one edge per pending wake, each naming a sender run, a
receiver run, and what it is waiting for. The receiver named on those edges has
not run at all, which is consistent with the parked node upstream of it.

Asked without a frame, the route answers 400 rather than guessing which frame
was meant.

## Who holds the claim

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/claim-handles/$CLAIM_HANDLE_ID/holders"
```

One holder — the parked node's run, still active. That is why the claim has not
come back. Together with the park roster this closes the loop: the same run is
the parked node and the claim holder, so an operator names the cause rather than
the symptom.

## The diagnostics report; they do not remediate

None of the four reads has a matching write action.

`POST /v1/nodes/{id}/reset` answers 409 —
`reset only valid when node has a failed terminal run in some scope`. There is
no un-park route, and `rimsky parked` offers only `list`. Held-frame release and
cancel, producer-outbox retry and drain, and wait-set clear are all 404; DELETE
on the wait-set route is 405.

The instance-level levers do not help either. `POST /v1/instances/{id}/resume`
answers 409 on an unpaused instance, and the node stays parked. The debug
override is refused until the instance is paused, then applies — and the node is
still parked afterwards.

The one action that clears the findings is
`POST /v1/instances/{id}/terminate`, after which the rosters no longer name the
instance because the instance is gone.
